title: Land is not a commodity: why a land value tax can cure the housing crisis
dek: The housing shortage is only the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.
why: The land value tax is an overlooked lever that both left- and right-wing economists agree on. Lars Doucet uses cases like Houston parking lots, Korea's assessment system, and Norway's resource dividend to turn an abstract tax into a story of power struggle.
who: Economists concerned with housing policy, urban planners, real estate developers, and investors and policy researchers who want to know whether a 'land tax' is worth betting on.

points.h: A land tax is not a property tax; it is a location tax
points.body: Lars uses an analogy to set up his argument: the land value tax shares a root with ordinary property tax, but splits 'building value' from 'land value.' A building tax punishes you for building, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax punishes you only for occupying a good location and letting it grow weeds. He says the value of land comes from the labor of the people around you—the fact that you can step out your door to work, go to school, and make friends depends on your neighbors and the whole city. Landlords lie back and siphon this collective value into their own pockets. This is the paradox of 'Progress and Poverty': a ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does that.

points.h: The build-more camp is right, but not enough
points.body: The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell—do we still need a land tax? Lars admits the 'housing shortage' is the main cause, but he points out that the YIMBY camp has not explained a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet the city center still has a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together, so the more you build, the more you pay, while hoarding and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. Developers thus have no incentive to develop, only to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says that without land tax reform, you end up in a stalemate: 'You changed the zoning, but I still won't sell.'

points.h: The objections are born of imagination
points.body: Lars groups the opposition into three categories and dismantles each. How do you separate land from buildings in assessment? He says about 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels every year and produces a nationwide land value map in five months; Norway uses the national property data platform Finn.no to train an automated valuation model for the whole country, with a core team of just three people. Worried about protests? He says the real source of protest is 'my land looks the same as my neighbor's, why do I pay more?' Under a land tax, your assessment basis is the same location as your neighbor's, so it is actually easier to calculate. The excuse for not implementing is that it has not been measured.

points.h: Little old ladies are not a reason to object
points.body: The sharpest criticism is 'transition unfairness'—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalization of all future tax liabilities, which is equivalent to a one-time expropriation. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: action is never a one-step national 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly who fear being driven out of their homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it first, and after death it is deducted from the estate with interest.

points.h: Britain's failure is a capacity problem
points.body: The most common counterexample online is Britain's 'People's Budget' of the 1910s: valuation took six years and was overturned by shopkeeper protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-discussed article is 'drawing a universal law from a sample of one,' and it simultaneously claims 'a pure land tax has never succeeded' and 'land cannot be valued'—yet Korea has been assessing the entire national land value parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves that Britain's state capacity was weak, not that the land tax is theoretically infeasible. His tone sharpens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as settled truth.

points.h: Norway achieves Georgism through resource dividends
points.body: Lars points to a fact that makes today's Norway a 'success story': the entire Norwegian resource management system is Georgist in structure—oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, extractors pay a very high resource tax, but production and investment themselves are not penalized, thus encouraging entrepreneurship while channeling the natural dividend into the state treasury to subsidize universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it does not apply to land value tax. This 'Norwegian paradox' leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can become its foundation.

points.h: The automobile opened a second frontier
points.body: Lars explains why the land question that filled the headlines 100 years ago disappeared: the frontier itself was a kind of 'free land' mechanism—as long as you could expand into the wilderness, the lower classes did not have to face the squeeze of 'high work plus high rent.' America's first frontier was the westward movement; after it closed came Henry George. In the 20th century, the automobile turned the suburbs into a 'second frontier,' extending the reprieve for another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006–2008. He says some now call this the 'second Gilded Age,' but it is just the same script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and the post-pandemic remote work as a 'third frontier' lasted only about five minutes before capital digested it.

points.h: Don't win online; do homework for politicians
points.body: The closing answer is pragmatic: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past five years is not to argue with keyboard warriors, but to anticipate every objection a state senator or city councilor might raise, prepare data simulations and answers in advance, and hand them directly to their office—he says 'doing homework for politicians' is an absurd but remarkably effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

terms.def: An annual tax levied on the value of land rather than the total value of property; it does not penalize building improvements.
The movement founded by Henry George in the 19th century: land is common wealth, and ground rent should be collected for society.
The movement advocating for loosening zoning restrictions and allowing more housing construction.
Using uniform models and sample parcels to automatically value all properties in a jurisdiction, rather than doing site-by-site physical assessments.
The Georgist ideal: tax only land value, and eliminate other taxes on labor and capital.
The high rent extracted from natural resources (such as oil), collected for the benefit of all citizens.
